- update-config: Use this skill to configure the Claude Code harness via settings.json. Automated behaviors ("from now on when X", "each time X", "whenever X", "before/after X") require hooks configured in settings.json - the harness executes these, not Claude, so memory/preferences cannot fulfill them. Also use for: permissions ("allow X", "add permission", "move permission to"), env vars ("set X=Y"), hook troubleshooting, or any changes to settings.json/settings.local.json files. Examples: "allow npm commands", "add bq permission to global settings", "move permission to user settings", "set DEBUG=true", "when claude stops show X". For simple settings like theme/model, suggest the /config command.
- keybindings-help: Use when the user wants to customize keyboard shortcuts, rebind keys, add chord bindings, or modify ~/.claude/keybindings.json. Examples: "rebind ctrl+s", "add a chord shortcut", "change the submit key", "customize keybindings".
- simplify: Review changed code for reuse, quality, and efficiency, then fix any issues found.
- fewer-permission-prompts: Scan your transcripts for common read-only Bash and MCP tool calls, then add a prioritized allowlist to project .claude/settings.json to reduce permission prompts.
- loop: Run a prompt or slash command on a recurring interval (e.g. /loop 5m /foo). Omit the interval to let the model self-pace. - When the user wants to set up a recurring task, poll for status, or run something repeatedly on an interval (e.g. "check the deploy every 5 minutes", "keep running /babysit-prs"). Do NOT invoke for one-off tasks.
- schedule: Create, update, list, or run scheduled remote agents (routines) that execute on a cron schedule. - When the user wants to schedule a recurring remote agent, set up automated tasks, create a cron job for Claude Code, or manage their scheduled agents/routines. Also use when the user wants a one-time scheduled run ("run this once at 3pm", "remind me to check X tomorrow").
- claude-api: Build, debug, and optimize Claude API / Anthropic SDK apps. Apps built with this skill should include prompt caching. Also handles migrating existing Claude API code between Claude model versions (4.5 → 4.6, 4.6 → 4.7, retired-model replacements).
TRIGGER when: code imports `anthropic`/`@anthropic-ai/sdk`; user asks for the Claude API, Anthropic SDK, or Managed Agents; user adds/modifies/tunes a Claude feature (caching, thinking, compaction, tool use, batch, files, citations, memory) or model (Opus/Sonnet/Haiku) in a file; questions about prompt caching / cache hit rate in an Anthropic SDK project.
SKIP: file imports `openai`/other-provider SDK, filename like `*-openai.py`/`*-generic.py`, provider-neutral code, general programming/ML.
- init: Initialize a new CLAUDE.md file with codebase documentation
- review: Review a pull request
- security-review: Complete a security review of the pending changes on the current branch

1	\section{Experiments}
2	\label{sec:experiments}
3	
4	\subsection{Experimental Setup}
5	\label{sec:setup}
6	
7	\paragraph{Datasets.}
8	We evaluate on three English NER benchmarks spanning a difficulty gradient, each serving a distinct role.
9	\textbf{SciERC} \cite{luan2018scierc} (551 test instances, 6 entity types) is the primary medium-difficulty test bed where models achieve ${\approx}$65\% F1.
10	\textbf{CoNLL-2003} \cite{tjongkimsang2003conll} (3{,}453 test sentences, 4 entity types, ${\approx}$91\% F1) serves as a ceiling-effect control where limited oracle headroom constrains selection gains.
11	\textbf{WNUT-17} \cite{derczynski2017wnut} (1{,}287 social media instances, 52\% zero F1) probes the signal-collapse boundary where model capability is insufficient.
12	
13	\paragraph{Models and sampling.}
14	Both \textbf{Qwen3-8B} and \textbf{LLaMA-3.1-8B-Instruct} are fine-tuned with LoRA (rank$=$32, $\alpha{=}64$) for 5 epochs using LLaMA Factory \cite{zheng2024llamafactory} under identical training procedures.
15	Qwen3-8B's SciERC checkpoint has a minor train--test mismatch (empty thinking tokens); a quantitative analysis rules out this confound (Appendix~\ref{app:thinking_token}).
16	We draw $N{=}8$ samples at $T{=}1.0$ (primary), with $N{=}16$ for scaling experiments.\footnote{$N{=}16$ with 3 seeds verifies scaling and ranking stability ($\sigma{\leq}0.026$; Table~\ref{tab:multiseed}); gains beyond $N{=}8$ are sublinear (Appendix~\ref{app:n_scaling}).}
17	Inference uses vLLM with constrained decoding \cite{willard2023guided}.\footnote{Quality estimation uses a single primary seed (seed${=}42$); selection uses 2-seed averages for variance estimation. Three-seed experiments ($\sigma{\leq}0.026$; Table~\ref{tab:multiseed}) confirm ranking stability; the reduced seed count for primary results reflects computational budget.}
18	
19	%% ============================================================
20	\subsection{Quality Estimation Results}
21	\label{sec:qe_results}
22	
23	\begin{table*}[t]
24	\centering
25	\small
26	\caption{NER quality estimation ($\rho$ and AUROC; $N{=}8$, primary seed${=}42$; 3-seed stability $\sigma{\leq}0.026$ in Table~\ref{tab:multiseed}). Best in \textbf{bold}. RE results in Appendix~\ref{app:re_extension}. $N{=}16$ in Table~\ref{tab:robustness}.}
27	\label{tab:quality_estimation}
28	\begin{tabular}{ll cc cc cc}
29	\toprule
30	& & \multicolumn{2}{c}{\textbf{SciERC}} & \multicolumn{2}{c}{\textbf{CoNLL (Qwen)}} & \multicolumn{2}{c}{\textbf{CoNLL (LLaMA)}} \\
31	\cmidrule(lr){3-4} \cmidrule(lr){5-6} \cmidrule(lr){7-8}
32	Signal & Family & $\rho$ & AUC & $\rho$ & AUC & $\rho$ & AUC \\
33	\midrule
34	VC & Structural & \textbf{.379} & \textbf{.663} & .424 & .789 & .426 & .709 \\
35	SJ  & Structural & .360 & .650 & .436 & .801 & \textbf{.431} & .704 \\
36	FK & Surface & .267 & .602 & .400 & .774 & .428 & .703 \\
37	EM  & Surface    & .295 & .614 & \textbf{.451} & \textbf{.816} & \textbf{.431} & .705 \\
38	\midrule
39	LP     & Model      & .205 & .578 & .316 & .753 & .307 & \textbf{.761} \\
40	\bottomrule
41	\end{tabular}
42	\end{table*}
43	
44	Table~\ref{tab:quality_estimation} presents $\rho$ and AUROC for five signals across tasks and models.\footnote{$\varepsilon{=}0.05$ applies only to selection (\S\ref{sec:selection_gap}); quality estimation is $\varepsilon$-free. Selection F1 is stable across $\varepsilon \in [0, 0.2]$ (Appendix~\ref{app:epsilon_robustness}).}
45	
46	\paragraph{Signal rankings are difficulty-dependent.}
47	On SciERC (medium difficulty), structural signals lead (VC $\rho{=}0.379$, SJ $0.360$) over surface ($\rho{\leq}0.295$) and LP ($0.205$); bootstrap CIs confirm the SJ--LP gap ($\Delta\rho{=}{+}0.155$; Appendix~\ref{app:bootstrap_signal}).
48	On CoNLL (ceiling-effect control, single-sample F1${\approx}$0.91), EM leads both $\rho$ and AUROC ($0.816$); the $\rho$--AUROC dissociation across datasets reflects use-case alignment.
49	At the signal-collapse boundary---WNUT-17 (macro F1${\approx}$42\%, 52\% zero-F1 instances)---full-set correlations are dominated by the zero/non-zero boundary: VC achieves $\rho{=}0.724$ (AUROC${=}0.913$) but conditional $\rho$ drops to 0.038 (Table~\ref{tab:wnut}).
50	LP shows the reverse pattern (full-set $\rho{=}{-}0.410$, conditional $\rho{=}0.350$), confirming that full-set correlations conflate binary success prediction with quality gradation.
51	Restricting to non-zero instances reshuffles rankings, with EM strongest ($\rho{=}0.360$; Figure~\ref{fig:signal_heatmap}).
52	
53	\begin{table}[t]
54	\centering
55	\small
56	\caption{Quality estimation on WNUT-17 (Qwen, $N{=}16$, $T{=}1.0$, $n{=}689$). Cond: non-zero F1 instances ($n{=}334$). Full-set $\rho$ reflects binary success prediction; conditional $\rho$ measures quality gradation. LP's conditional $\rho$ is highest despite negative full-set $\rho$.}
57	\label{tab:wnut}
58	\begin{tabular}{lcccc}
59	\toprule
60	Signal & $\rho$ & AUROC & Cond.\ $\rho$ & Cond.\ $p$ \\
61	\midrule
62	VC      & .724 & .913 & .038 & .487 \\
63	FK      & .125 & .555 & .169 & .002 \\
64	SJ      & .089 & .517 & .288 & ${<}$1e-7 \\
65	EM      & .050 & .487 & .333 & ${<}$1e-9 \\
66	LP & $-$.410 & .219 & .350 & ${<}$1e-10 \\
67	\bottomrule
68	\end{tabular}
69	\end{table}
70	
71	%% ============================================================
72	\subsection{The Correlation-Selection Gap}
73	\label{sec:selection_gap}
74	
75	We define the correlation-selection gap as the disparity between a signal's instance-level rank correlation with F1 and its ability to select the best output from $N$ candidates.
76	
77	\begin{table}[t]
78	\centering
79	\small
80	\caption{Best-of-$N$ NER selection (macro F1) on SciERC ($N{=}8$, $T{=}1.0$, 2-seed mean${\pm}\sigma$, $p$ vs.\ greedy baseline from paired sign tests). LP is per-sample; others use consensus-proximity. Best non-oracle in \textbf{bold}. Random: uniform random selection from $N$ candidates. Non-tied LP subset analysis in \S\ref{sec:discussion}; RE selection in Appendix~\ref{app:re_extension}.}
81	\label{tab:selection}
82	\begin{tabular}{lcc}
83	\toprule
84	Method & NER F1 & $p$ \\
85	\midrule
86	Oracle & $0.778 \pm 0.003$ & --- \\
87	Greedy ($T{=}0$) & $0.645 \pm 0.001$ & --- \\
88	\midrule
89	\multicolumn{3}{l}{\textit{Per-sample signal}} \\
90	LP           & $\mathbf{0.647} \pm 0.005$ & .29 \\
91	\midrule
92	\multicolumn{3}{l}{\textit{Instance-level signals (consensus-proximity selection)}} \\
93	SJ           & $0.646 \pm 0.002$ & .67 \\
94	FK           & $0.646 \pm 0.001$ & .79 \\
95	EM           & $0.637 \pm 0.001$ & --- \\
96	VC           & $0.623 \pm 0.004$ & --- \\
97	\midrule
98	Random           & $0.610 \pm 0.003$ & --- \\
99	\bottomrule
100	\end{tabular}
101	\end{table}
102	
103	Despite moderate quality estimation, confidence signals yield limited selection gains (Table~\ref{tab:selection}, Figure~\ref{fig:selection_gap}).
104	Instance-level signals (SJ, FK, EM, VC) assign identical QE scores to all candidates per input; consensus-proximity (MBR) converts these to per-sample rankings (Table~\ref{tab:selection}: SJ 0.646, FK 0.646, EM 0.637, VC 0.623), but none improves over the greedy baseline.
105	The key question is whether LP---the only natively per-sample signal---can exploit the oracle headroom.
106	
107	\paragraph{No significant improvement over greedy.}
108	On SciERC NER (2-seed sign tests\footnote{Multi-seed NER experiments confirm seed variation is small ($\sigma{\leq}0.026$; Table~\ref{tab:multiseed}).}, $n{=}529$), the oracle (0.778) reveals 13.3~pp of headroom above greedy (0.645), yet LP achieves only 0.647 ($\Delta{=}{+}0.2$~pp, $p{=}0.29$); no signal consistently improves selection ($p{>}0.05$; TOST equivalence holds under all external anchors for LLaMA-CoNLL but varies by configuration, Appendix~\ref{app:tost}).
109	The pattern holds across CoNLL and WNUT-17 (Table~\ref{tab:cross_selection}); RE selection results are consistent (Appendix~\ref{app:re_extension}).
110	CoNLL's near-ceiling single-sample F1 (0.91) with only ${\sim}$4~pp oracle headroom functions primarily as a ceiling-effect control.
111	Under stringent external TOST anchors ($\delta_0{=}1.0$~pp), some configurations (e.g., Qwen CoNLL) show statistically significant degradation, indicating signals can actively harm selection (Appendix~\ref{app:tost}).
112	LP approximately matches greedy decoding ($T{=}0$; $\Delta{=}{+}0.2$~pp, not significant); neither significantly outperforms the other, yet both fall far short of the oracle (0.778, 13.3~pp gap).
113	Instance-level signals predict \textit{which inputs} the model handles reliably, not \textit{which output} is best; closing this gap likely requires trained verifiers \cite{cobbe2021verifiers}.\footnote{For negative results (all $p{>}0.05$), uncorrected tests suffice; the sole positive finding (non-tied LP subset, $+2.9$~pp, $p{=}0.004$; \S\ref{sec:discussion}) survives Bonferroni correction over 5 comparisons.}
114	
115	%% ============================================================
116	\subsection{Robustness}
117	\label{sec:robustness_main}
118	
119	Consistency signals are robust across $T{\in}\{0.7, 1.0\}$ with sublinear $N$-scaling gains (Table~\ref{tab:robustness}); LP shows the largest temperature sensitivity ($\Delta\rho{=}{+}0.044$).
120	Signal rankings are stable across seeds (Kendall's $W{=}1.0$ at $N{=}8$; Table~\ref{tab:ranking-stability}).
121	NER calibration is reasonable (ECE 0.069--0.096; Appendix~\ref{app:calibration}).
122	
123	\begin{table}[t]
124	\centering
125	\small
126	\caption{Scale ablation: Qwen3-8B vs.\ 4B NER quality estimation ($\rho$; $N{=}8$, $T{=}1.0$, seed${=}42$). 8B values identical to Table~\ref{tab:quality_estimation}; 4B uses matched evaluation protocol. RE scale ablation in Appendix~\ref{app:re_extension}.}
127	\label{tab:scale_ablation}
128	\begin{tabular}{@{}ll cc r@{}}
129	\toprule
130	& & \textbf{8B} & \textbf{4B} & $\Delta$ \\
131	\midrule
132	CoNLL & SJ & .436 & .422 & $-$.014 \\
133	      & FK & .400 & .418 & $+$.018 \\
134	SciERC & SJ & .360 & .422 & $+$.062 \\
135	       & FK & .267 & .326 & $+$.059 \\
136	\bottomrule
137	\end{tabular}
138	\end{table}
139	
140	\paragraph{Scale robustness.}
141	Repeating with Qwen3-4B (Table~\ref{tab:scale_ablation}), quality estimation is comparable or improved (mean $|\Delta\rho|{=}0.042$), yet selection remains below greedy on SciERC ($\Delta$ up to $-3.4$~pp) despite 13.0~pp of oracle headroom, and indistinguishable on CoNLL (${<}0.3$~pp, 1.7~pp headroom). Within the 3B--8B range tested across two model families, task difficulty is a stronger predictor of the gap than model scale.
142	Instance degeneracy also scales with model capability: 8B shows twice the degeneracy of 4B on SciERC (21\% vs.\ 10.4\%) despite comparable within-instance utility correlation (Table~\ref{tab:degeneracy}).
143	
144	\paragraph{LoRA-rank ablation.}
145	To disentangle model capacity from degeneracy, we train Qwen3-8B on SciERC with LoRA rank${=}8$ (vs.\ rank${=}32$ in all other experiments).
146	Reducing rank lowers degeneracy from 21\% to 7.2\% and increases oracle headroom from 13.3~pp to 16.0~pp, confirming that fine-tuning capacity drives output convergence.
147	However, selection still fails: the best signal (LP, 0.635) falls short of greedy (0.640), and all consensus-proximity signals perform worse (SJ 0.631, VC 0.592).
148	Quality estimation remains comparable (VC $\rho{=}0.394$ vs.\ $0.379$; SJ $\rho{=}0.365$ vs.\ $0.360$).
149	Low degeneracy is thus a necessary but not sufficient condition for selection---LP compression persists regardless of LoRA rank, indicating that both mechanisms must be addressed simultaneously.
150	
151	\paragraph{Supervised verifier baseline.}
152	To test whether the information bottleneck lies in the aggregation method or the features themselves, we train a logistic regression verifier on all five signals (3-fold cross-validation on SciERC, $N{=}8$).
153	The supervised selector achieves F1${=}0.648$, closing only 0.8\% of the oracle gap---a negligible improvement over the best unsupervised signal (LP, 0.647; $\Delta{=}{+}0.08$~pp).
154	Its AUROC (0.697) is lower than single-signal VC (0.706), and feature importance is dominated by VC (coefficient 0.65--0.92) with SJ receiving a negative coefficient.
155	The failure of supervised signal combination confirms that the bottleneck is not in how signals are aggregated but in what information they encode: these features lack per-sample discriminative content sufficient for selection.

\section{Discussion}\label{sec:discussion}

\paragraph{Implications for practitioners.}
VC leads on medium-difficulty NER ($\rho{=}0.379$, SciERC); EM leads easy NER and binary discrimination (AUROC${=}0.816$, CoNLL).
Rankings hold across model families and a 4B ablation (Table~\ref{tab:scale_ablation}); at the capability boundary (WNUT-17), all signals collapse. RE signal rankings are reported in Appendix~\ref{app:re_extension}.

\paragraph{Why the gap exists.}
We identify two mechanisms: \textit{instance degeneracy} (affecting consensus-proximity selection) and \textit{LP compression} (affecting per-sample selection).

Within-instance analysis (restricted to non-degenerate instances where F1 varies across samples) reveals that MBR utility \cite{eikema2022sampling} does correlate positively with F1 (SJ median within-instance $\rho{=}0.524$ on SciERC, $0.994$ on CoNLL), and on these instances consensus-proximity selection closes 23\% (SciERC) to 41\% (CoNLL) of the oracle gap.

CoNLL (91\% single-sample F1) exhibits 58\% degeneracy; SciERC (66\%) shows 21\%; WNUT-17 (${\approx}$42\%, macro) shows near-zero---the tension between model quality and selection utility is inherent.
Scale ablation confirms this tension: Qwen3-8B shows 21\% instance degeneracy on SciERC vs.\ 10.4\% for the weaker Qwen3-4B, despite comparable within-instance utility correlation ($\rho{=}0.52$ vs.\ $0.55$; Table~\ref{tab:degeneracy}).
Despite MBR's success in machine translation \cite{freitag2022high}, all variants fail here because degeneracy eliminates the headroom that positive within-instance correlation would otherwise exploit (Appendix~\ref{app:mbr_discussion}).
Meanwhile, LP selection approximately matches greedy decoding ($T{=}0$; $\Delta{=}{+}0.2$~pp, $p{=}0.29$; Table~\ref{tab:selection}), and both fall far short of the oracle (0.778, 13.3~pp gap)---multi-sample selection adds cost without closing the gap.

\paragraph{Non-tied subset analysis.}
Where compression is mitigated, LP selection works.
Restricting to instances with LP range ${\geq}0.05$ ($n{=}210$, 40\% of total; Table~\ref{tab:nontied_main}), within-instance $\rho(\text{LP}, \text{F1})$ rises from 0.08 (tied subset) to 0.39 (non-tied), and LP selection outperforms greedy by $+2.9$~pp ($p{=}0.004$).

However, the effect size is sensitive to subset definition, and the non-tied subset constitutes only 40\% of instances, limiting practical impact.

\paragraph{Signal combinations.}
We test three LP${\times}$VC combination strategies: VC-stratified LP selection, LP${\times}$VC product ranking, and LP tiebreaking within VC-equivalent groups.
All three fail to improve over greedy (best: $+0.2$~pp, $p{>}0.3$), consistent with VC's collapse on degenerate instances and LP's compression on the remainder.
An oracle tiebreaker---selecting the highest-F1 sample among VC-equivalent candidates---recovers $+7.9$~pp, confirming that per-sample signal \textit{exists} within VC-equivalent groups but current signals cannot extract it.

\paragraph{Hypotheses for LP compression.}
We identify four (non-mutually-exclusive) mechanisms that may explain within-instance LP compression, though we do not isolate their individual contributions.
Two are \textit{constraint-imposed}:
(b) \textit{schema-dominated tokens}---constrained decoding enforces structural tokens (brackets, type labels) that carry no extraction information yet dominate the sequence, reducing effective variance;
(c) \textit{vocabulary restriction}---constrained decoding shrinks the effective vocabulary at each step, concentrating probability mass and reducing log-probability variation.
Two are \textit{model-learned}:
(a) \textit{token-level averaging}---mean log-probability over long sequences smooths token-level variance, compressing the effective signal;
(d) \textit{format-token dilution}---fine-tuned models assign extremely high LP to schema tokens (\texttt{\{"entities": [}~etc.) that carry no extraction information, diluting the signal from entity-name tokens; free-form parse rates of 99.95\% confirm that format tokens dominate the sequence.

Removing grammar constraints (SciERC NER, Qwen3-8B, 4 seeds) yields nearly identical LP distributions (std ratio 0.97) and negligible selection changes (Appendix~\ref{app:freeform_ablation}), ruling out constrained decoding as the cause of NER compression.
On RE, free-form decoding consistently reverses LP selection direction ($+1.8{\pm}0.1$~pp, 4 seeds), suggesting regime-dependent behavior (Appendix~\ref{app:re_extension}).
VC becomes per-sample in the selection context (each candidate's overlap with the majority-voted output varies), yet tends to select the most typical rather than the best output---consistent with MBR's known mode-seeking bias \cite{eikema2022sampling, deguchi2024centroid}.
More broadly, all consensus-proximity strategies fail because instance degeneracy eliminates the headroom that positive within-instance correlation would otherwise exploit (Table~\ref{tab:degeneracy}; Appendix~\ref{app:mbr_discussion}).

\paragraph{Ablation: entity-token LP.}
We directly test hypothesis (d) by isolating entity-mention tokens from the log-probability computation.
On SciERC, entity-token LP exhibits $4{\times}$ higher within-instance variance than full-sequence LP, confirming that format tokens do compress the signal.
However, entity-token LP selection performs \textit{worse} than full-sequence LP ($-2.0$~pp), and on CoNLL, entity-token LP variance collapses to near-zero (median $2{\times}10^{-10}$) with 79\% of instances tied---consistent with CoNLL's limited entity vocabulary (4 types, high-frequency names) that fine-tuning drives to near-deterministic prediction.
This rules out format-token dilution as the primary cause of LP's selection failure and instead points to an intrinsic pattern: fine-tuned models assign near-deterministic probabilities to entity-name tokens themselves, leaving minimal discriminative signal regardless of aggregation scope.

\paragraph{Pilot remedy.}
Entity-token LP represents a natural pilot remedy: if format-token dilution caused compression, restricting LP to entity tokens should recover selection ability.
Its failure---particularly the near-zero entity-token variance on CoNLL---suggests that effective remedies must address the underlying model confidence calibration rather than signal aggregation.

\paragraph{Practical considerations.}
Multi-sample inference incurs $N{\times}$ compute cost.
For quality estimation---where signals are already reliable ($\rho$ up to 0.45 on CoNLL, 0.42 on the primary test bed; AUROC up to 0.82)---$N{=}8$ samples suffice (Appendix~\ref{app:n_scaling}), making the cost acceptable for selective prediction or error flagging in high-stakes IE.
For selection, the cost-benefit is unfavorable: $8{\times}$ inference yields at most $+0.2$~pp over greedy ($p{>}0.05$).
Whether the trade-off shifts in low-convergence regimes (e.g., under-parameterized models where degeneracy drops below 10\%) remains an open question.

\paragraph{Methodological implications.}
The decoupling of $\rho$, AUROC, and selection F1 means single-metric evaluation risks selecting the wrong signal.
Even supervised combination of all five signals closes ${<}1\%$ of the oracle gap (\S\ref{sec:robustness_main}), confirming the information bottleneck is in the features themselves, not the aggregation method.
Effective selection thus requires content-aware verifiers that examine output semantics \cite{cobbe2021verifiers, venktesh2025trust}, not confidence signal aggregation; $N{=}8$ captures most quality estimation benefit (Appendix~\ref{app:n_scaling}).

\begin{abstract}
Self-consistency yields large gains on discrete-answer tasks, but named entity recognition (NER) produces \textit{sets} of entities with partial overlap, where no majority vote analog exists.
We evaluate five confidence signals---four instance-level (structural and surface agreement) and one per-sample (log-probability)---for quality estimation and sample selection on three NER benchmarks spanning a difficulty gradient (SciERC, CoNLL, WNUT-17), using 4B--8B models.
All signals achieve reliable quality estimation ($\rho$ up to 0.45 on CoNLL, 0.42 on the primary test bed; AUROC up to 0.82), supporting selective prediction and error flagging.
However, quality estimation does not translate to sample selection---the \textit{correlation-selection gap}: best-of-$N$ selection approximately matches greedy decoding ($T{=}0$) despite 13--18~pp oracle headroom.
We diagnose two mechanisms: (a)~\textit{instance degeneracy}---fine-tuned models produce identical outputs for 21--58\% of instances, eliminating selection headroom despite positive within-instance utility--F1 correlation (median $\rho{=}0.52$); and (b)~\textit{log-probability compression}---median within-instance range of 0.041 nats, with entity-token isolation revealing intrinsic overconfidence rather than format-token dilution.
A five-layer ablation chain and a LoRA-rank ablation (degeneracy 7\% vs.\ 21\%) confirm these mechanisms are intrinsic to capable fine-tuned models: reducing degeneracy is necessary but not sufficient for selection.
Closing the gap likely requires learned per-sample scoring.
\end{abstract}

That could explain the variation. The exp-027 analysis uses cross-validation with train/test splits, which is a different evaluation protocol than using the full dataset like Table 1 does, so the absolute values being lower makes sense.

What matters most here is that exp-027 confirms MLP doesn't improve over logistic regression, which aligns with the paper's core finding that the bottleneck is in feature quality, not the aggregation method.

\paragraph{Supervised verifier baseline.}
To test whether the information bottleneck lies in the aggregation method or the features themselves, we train a logistic regression verifier on all five signals (3-fold cross-validation on SciERC, $N{=}8$).
The supervised selector achieves F1${=}0.648$, closing only 0.8\% of the oracle gap---a negligible improvement over the best unsupervised signal (LP, 0.647; $\Delta{=}{+}0.08$~pp).
Its AUROC (0.697) is lower than single-signal VC (0.706), and feature importance is dominated by VC (coefficient 0.65--0.92) with SJ receiving a negative coefficient.
The failure of supervised signal combination confirms that the bottleneck is not in how signals are aggregated but in what information they encode: these features lack per-sample discriminative content sufficient for selection.
